list.listitem: Children suspected of having juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) should be referred to a subspecialist (pediatric rheumatologist or orthopedist) as early as possible. C
Children with JIA are at risk for asymptomatic uveitis and should be screened by an ophthalmologist.

Additional treatment options for JIA include disease modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs), intra-articular corticosteroids, systemic corticosteroids, and biologics such as canakinumab, anakinra, or tofacitinib. B

background.definition: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is arthritis of at least 6 weeks' duration occurring in children younger than 16 years. Subtypes are characterized by the number of joints involved and other clinical signs and symptoms.

list.listitem: 0.008 to 0.226 per 1000 children worldwide.
0.07 to 4.01 per 1000 children worldwide.

Including costs concerning medication use, visits to specialists and allied health professionals, and diagnostic tests, the total difference in annualized average direct medical costs for children with juvenile arthritis versus controls (children without juvenile arthritis seen in outpatient clinics) is approximately US$1500.
Most common rheumatic disease of childhood.
Chronic inflammatory condition of multifactorial etiology- both genetic and environmental contributing causes.
Several genetic risk/loci have been identified conferring increased susceptibility to JIA.
Inflammatory cytokines including interleukin 1, IL-6, and tumor necrosis factor-α stimulate the release of proteinases.
Destruction of bone and cartilage follows the increased inflammatory response.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Two peaks ages- toddler to preschool age and adolescence
More common in females than in males 3:1

list.listitem: Screen for TB prior to starting biologic disease modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARD) or when there is a possible exposure to TB.
Age appropriate immunizations (other than live attenuated vaccines for immunosuppressed children) are recommended.
The diagnosis of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is usually made clinically.
CBC and sed rate are recommended as initial diagnostic tests to rule out other pathology.
No laboratory studies are diagnostic for JIA.
A thorough history and physical are important in making the diagnosis.
Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) is a life threatening complication of systemic JIA. Affected patients may develop abnormal bleeding and cardiac, liver, or renal failure.

Differential.Differential_Name: Benign nocturnal limb pains of childhood "growing pains"
Differential.Differential_Features: Cramping lower-leg pain in the evenings or nights
Constitutional symptoms, ill appearance, nonarticular bone pain
Tenderness at tendon insertion, worse at the end of day, does not limit activities
Lumbar back pain and stiffness, HLA-B27 positive
Arthritis follows GI or genitourinary infection; painful iritis classic
Chronic or recurrent abdominal pain, malaise
Painful symmetric arthritis, rash, lymphadenopathy, high ANA

list.listitem: Chronic arthritis lasting 6 weeks in a least 1 joint and with exclusion of other causes or symptoms.
Patients typically present with swelling or synovitis involving one or more joints.
Joint involvement is typically painless, but can be painful.
Other physical findings might include muscle weakness, atrophy, bony overgrowth, leg length discrepancy, retro/micrognathia.
See for more detailed diagnostic criteria.
Complete blood count (CBC) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) are recommended for children with chronic joint pain to help exclude infection and other pathology.
ESR may be normal in children with juvenile arthritis, and elevation cannot discriminate among different etiologies of inflammation.
Serum calprotectin levels have been found in inflammatory chronic diseases and may correlate with ESR, CRP, and disease activity in JIA.
Since patients with a positive ANA are at higher risk for developing silent uveitis, patients should be screened for ANA.
40-50% of JIA can be ANA negative.
Changes on plain radiographs early in the disease course are nonspecific, and late radiographic changes are often irreversible.
MRI has the greatest sensitivity for inflammatory processes but may be time consuming and more expensive.
Ultrasound and MRI might identify synovitis but can not always determine the cause.
Progression of joint damage as seen by plain radiography was most pronounced in the wrist and MCP joints among 186 children with JRA aged 1 to 10 years.

ACR 2021 guidelines recommend CBC, LFTs and renal function every 6 to 12 months for children on medical therapy. For children on methotrexate, sulfasalazine, leflunomide, canakinumab, anakinra, or tofacitinib, these tests are recommended within the first month and every 3 to 4 months thereafter.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to the child with musculoskeletal pain.
Goals of therapy include relieving pain, preserving joint range of motion and function, minimizing systemic complications, and promoting normal growth and development. C
Cognitive-behavioral therapy may be used to reduce pain and psychological disability and to enhance self-efficacy and pain coping. B
Children with a presumptive diagnosis of JIA should be referred to a subspecialists and mutidisciplinary team, if possible, for assistance with ongoing management. C
Medication treatment options include NSAIDS, DMARDs, intra-articular corticosteroids, systemic corticosteroids and biologics such as canakinumab, anakinra, or tofacitinib. B
Recommend rapid and aggressive therapy to control inflammation, then gradual taper of medications after remission.
More fequent opthalmologic monitoring in patients wirh controlled uveitis is recommended.
Monitoring within 1 month after each change of topical glucocorticoids, within 2 months tapering or discontinuing systemic therapy and at least every 3 months in patients on stable therapy
In JIA polyarthritis, initial therapy with DMARDS is recommended over NSAIDS given as a single therapy.
NSAIDS or intrarticular glucocorticoids are conditionally recommended as an adjunct treatment- low evidence.
Treatment with a combination of biologic therapies and a DMARD is conditionally recommended over the use of biologic agents alone. Biologic agents include canakinumab, anakinra, or tofacitinib.

A Cochrane review of tumor necrosis factor inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib, and upadacitinib) identified 9 RCTs with 678 participants. Treatment response at 16 weeks was higher (34% vs 14%, p < .05, NNT = 5) and mean pain scores on a 100 mm visual scale were lower (11 vs 33 mm). There was significant uncertainty around estimates of the effects on pain, function, and quality of life.
A systematc review of 7 observational studies of abatacept (a drug that interferes with T cell function) found low quality evidence of benefit.

A network meta-analysis of 10 RCTs with 898 participants found trials comparing infliximab, canakinumab, baricitinib, anakinra, adalimumab, tofacitinib, tocilizumab, and rilonacept. The authors concluded that canakinumab (which blocks interleukin-1 beta) was most likely to be effective.
Recomendations are against adding low dose glucocorticoids irrespective of risk factors or disease activity due to adverse side effects.

Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) limit long-term morbidity by controlling disease before irreversible joint damage occurs. Common DMARDs include methotrexate and sulfasalazine. The decision to treat with DMARDs should be reserved to subspecialists.
Children taking methotrexate should also be given folic acid supplements.
The use of etanercept among 61 children with JIA (mean age 10.6 years) was associated with improvements in health-related quality of life.
Anti-interleukin-1 therapy has been evaluated in several clinical trails of patients with JIA.

Among 112 children with severe persistent refractory JIA, tocilizumab (anti-interleukin-6 receptor antibody) was associated with an 85% improvement in response (as defined by an American College of Rheumatology core measures) compared to a 24% response rate in patients getting placebo. However, more patients in the tocilizumab group experienced adverse events such as infections than placebo patients. Other adverse events-included neutropenia and increased hepatic transaminase levels.

Canakinumab (an anti-interleukin-1β monoclonal antibody) was associated with a higher response rate than placebo (84% vs. 10%) among patients (aged 2-19) with JIA. As with tocilizumab, infections were more common in actively treated patients compared to placebo.

Rilonacept (an anti-interleukin-1 fusion protein) use was associated with clinical and laboratory improvements amongst 23 patients (mean age 14) in an open-label 23 month trial, and was associated with a decrease (or discontinuation) of prednisone in 22 or the 23 patients.
Use of biologics appears to reduce growth impairment in children with JIA.
Antidepressants are moderately helpful in managing the chronic pain of chronic rheumatoid arthritis, but have not been as well studied in children and adolescents.

Children with arthritis often keep their joints in a flexed position to minimize discomfort, and can develop weakness of extensor muscles and contracture of flexor muscles. The 2021 ACR guidelines conditionally recommend physical and occupational therapy for children with JIA.
Physical therapy and splinting might help to prevent flexion contractures.

A systematic review found 3 studies with 212 participants of exercise in JIA. No evidence of benefit or harm was found, but the small size of the studies makes it possible a clinically meaningful benefit could have been missed.

A randomized, placebo-controlled, single blinded study of a home exercise program found improvements in functional ability, pain, quality of life and the 6 minute walk test among 81 children with JIA.

Children with chronic arthritis are at risk for developing overall adjustment problems as well as internalizing symptoms of anxiety, depression, and social withdrawal. They are not at higher risk for poor self-concept or self-esteem problems compared to controls.
Cognitive-behavioral therapy might help reduce pain and psychological disability and enhance self-efficacy and pain coping.
The effect of diets (i.e., vegetarian, Mediterranean, and elimination) is uncertain based on a systematic review of 15 studies. A healthy age appropriate diet is recommended by ACR guidelines (2021).
The MMR booster vaccination is safe and effective in children with JRA.
Children suspected of having JIA should be referred to a subspecialist (pediatric rheumatologist or orthopedist) as early as possible.
Untreated or undertreated juvenile arthritis results in poor linear growth, osteoporosis, and leg length discrepancies. B
Approximately 50% of children with treated juvenile arthritis enter adulthood with active disease and functional limitation. B
Fewer than 10% of children with treated juvenile arthritis enter adulthood with severe disabilities. B

An inactive lifestyle in patients with JIA may be an important contributer to the development of subclinical signs of atherosclerosis. Promotion of an active lifestyle in childhood/adolescence may diminish the risk of atherosclerosis in adulthood.

cell.label: Take history and perform complete physical examination, focusing on (but not limited to) affected area, to look for evidence of systemic or other involvement. Obvious etiology of symptoms (e.g., trauma, sprain, strain, fracture)?
Normal activity and physical examination with no worsening symptoms and no constitutional or systemic complaints (e.g., fever, weight loss, rash)?
Underlying illness, immunosuppression, or constitutional complaints (e.g., fever, weight loss, fatigue)?
Consider: Infection (check CBC and ESR), malignancy (check CBC and ESR), and systemic lupus erythematosus (check CBC, ESR, and antinuclear antibodies).
Check CBC and ESR. Consider infection, malignancy, reactive arthritis, and trauma.

Check CBC, ESR and antinuclear antibodies: consider malar, nasal/oral, photosensitive, vasculitic (SLE). Check urinalysis and creatinine: consider Henoch-Schonlein purpura. Consider Erythema marginatum (acute rheumatic fever), Gottron’s papules (juvenile dermatomyositis), and psoriasis (psoriatic arthritis).
Check CBC, ESR, and possible synovial fluid analysis. Consider infection, JRA, reactive arthritis, malignancy, and spondyloarthropathy.
Consider JRA, spondyloarthropathy, SLE, Henoch-Schonlein purpura, and Lyme arthritis.
Reassurance or schedule follow-up if physician or parental concerns exist.

feature.caption: Diagnostic Criteria for Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis.
feature.feature_body: The American College of Rheumatology classififies types of of juvenile rheumatoid arthritis. They are distinguished by the number of affected joints, as well as other clinical symptoms: Oligoarticular- involving 4 joints or less Polyarticular- diminished use and joint swelling involving 5 or more joints RF(+) and RF(-) Psoriatic arthritis- arthritis and psoriasis ERA- arthritis and enthesitis Undifferated arthritis- fulfills criteria for no category or 2 or more categories Systemic-onset: daily fevers with high spikes, recurring evanescent erythematous rash, variable joint involvement, generalized lymphadenopathy From Cassidy JT, Levinson JE, Bass JC, et al. A study of classification criteria for a diagnosis of juvenile rheumatoid arthritis. Arthritis Rheum 1986;29:274–281; and Junnila JL, Cartwright VW. Chronic musculoskeletal pain in children: Part I: initial evaluation. Am Fam Phys 2006;74:115–122. and Shenoi, Susan.
